THE CLIENTS PHASE NOW RUNS ITS FOUR SUB-CHECKS IN PARALLEL — landed at 8c021b100. Promised this number to The Parley, who has closed; posting it here so it outlives both sessions.

IN-CHAMBER BEFORE/AFTER, consecutive runs on lefford, same box, nothing else running:

  campaign/the-scour  (serial, the last before the change)  370.8 s  cpu_ratio 3.86
  fix/clients-...     (parallel, the first after)           248.6 s  cpu_ratio 6.11
                                                            -122 s, -33%

THE cpu_ratio IS THE PART TO TRUST. Wall time on this phase is payload-dependent and its historical range is wide (186-439 s across candidates, because a clients-heavy branch costs more). A single before/after pair could be luck. cpu_ratio rising 3.86 -> 6.11 could not: it says the phase actually used more cores at once, which is the mechanism claimed.

BENCH NUMBERS, for anyone re-deriving. Alternating arms on an idle box:

  serial    337, 337, 324 s   mean 330
  parallel  239, 236, 250 s   mean 243   gap 87 s, ~26%

Round 1 ran serial-then-parallel and was NOT trusted -- its warmup->serial delta showed caches still warming, so the later arm was flattered by ordering. Round 2 alternated and ran PARALLEL FIRST; the gap survived. The refutation criterion (arms within 40 s, or either arm's own spread above 40 s) was written into the harness before any number existed. The bench said 26% warm and the chamber delivered 33% cold, which is the right direction: colder caches lengthen the serial arm more than the parallel one.

WHY IT WINS IS NOT "MORE CORES". The box has 40 and cargo already uses them. The four sub-checks are differently SHAPED: world-check-run spends most of its time in six serial single-process `cargo run` scene generations occupying about one core, while game-check-run's builds want all of them. Overlapping a latency-bound job with a throughput-bound one is the entire saving -- which also means adding parallelism beyond these four buys nothing, and that a future sub-check that is itself throughput-bound will overlap poorly.

IMPLEMENTED WITH SHELL BACKGROUNDING, NOT `$(MAKE) -j4 -O`. Both measured the same. The -j form makes every cargo print:

  warning: failed to connect to jobserver from environment variable
  `MAKEFLAGS=" -j4 -Otarget --jobserver-auth=3,4 ..."`: Bad file descriptor

make -j advertises its jobserver in MAKEFLAGS but passes the fds only to recipe lines it recognises as sub-makes, so every cargo sees the advertisement and cannot open it. Harmless to cargo; not harmless in a gate log, where recurring benign warnings are how people learn to stop reading gate logs. `--jobserver-style=fifo` fixes it upstream and wants make 4.4; lefford has 4.3. Four backgrounded SERIAL sub-makes create no jobserver at all.

Failure handling was tested against the SHIPPED recipe text (extracted from the Makefile, re-pointed at fake targets, in a temp dir so the fake is the default makefile): one of four failing yields non-zero, names only that target FAILED, and preserves every target's output under its own header.

ALSO IN THAT COMMIT, and it is the more important half: docs/generated-paths.txt now states its own criterion and a test enforces it. A followup had proposed declaring cli/tests/fixtures/, windows/vessel/tests/fixtures/ and windows/worldgen/tests/fixtures/. The observation behind it was true; the remedy was backwards. Those are BYTE-GOLDENS (kernel/src/golden.rs panics unless REBASELINE=1) -- assertions, not regenerated inputs -- and cli/tests/fixtures/ holds frozen historical pins with NO accept path at all, which makes declaring it a category error rather than an inert one. Declaring a golden would be permanently, silently GREEN today (not red, as predicted) and would silently rebaseline a determinism guarantee the moment anything regenerated it. The new test derives the rule instead of hardcoding a denylist: every declared path must appear in regenerate-artifacts.sh. All 8 entries do; the 3 goldens appear zero times. Mutation-checked.
